new_statements.quote: IV. EL ACENTO. El acento prosódico de la palabra recae generalmente en la penúltima sílaba. [...] V. CANTIDAD VOCALICA [...] 2. Para identificar una vocal larga hay que escuchar el ritmo de la palabra. Todas las sílabas tienen la misma duración excepto la de vocal larga y que por ser más larga también suena un poquito más fuerte. [...] 5. Otro fenómeno que tiene que ver con la cantidad vocálica es el hecho de que la primera persona se señala mediante la prolongación de la vocal. Cuando es sujeto se alarga la última vocal del verbo y cuando es posesivo se alarga la última vocal del sustantivo.
new_statements.translation: IV. STRESS. The prosodic stress of the word falls generally on the penultimate syllable. [...] V. VOWEL QUANTITY [...] 2. To identify a long vowel one must listen to the rhythm of the word. All syllables have the same duration except the long-vowel syllable, which, being longer, also sounds a little stronger. [...] 5. Another phenomenon related to vowel quantity is that first person is marked by lengthening the vowel: as subject, the last vowel of the verb is lengthened; as possessor, the last vowel of the noun.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is generally on the penultimate syllable. Long vowels (which in this variety occur only in open syllables and mark, among other things, first person by lengthening the word-final vowel) are said to sound somewhat stronger, so a word-final long vowel may carry perceptible prominence; the source hedges with 'generalmente' but names no specific exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated explicitly ('generalmente'). The remark that long-vowel syllables sound 'a little stronger', together with word-final 1st-person vowel length, is the likely exception class; Cerrón-Palomino 1987: 124-125 (comparative, second-hand for this lect) reports final-syllable accent on such Junín forms ([wasí:] 'my house').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('acento prosódico de la palabra'); citation forms in a pedagogical grammar; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1990 Lecciones describe the variety of south-east Pasco (Huachón, Paucartambo, Ninacaca, Huayllay) and the provinces of Junín and Tarma (preface, p. 5), which SIL tags as North Junín Quechua [qvn] = nort2980; Adelaar 1977 (the named-but-unreachable grammar) describes the Tarma-town dialect of the same language (WALS 'Quechua (Tarma)' qta -> nort2980). Cerrón-Palomino's 'juninense' remarks are about central (Junín) Quechua I generally and include Huanca (huay1241/jauj1238), so they are not a first-hand statement for nort2980.

sources.note: 'Pronunciación y ortografía' pp. 13-28; section 'IV. El acento' (p. 22) states that word stress falls generally on the penultimate syllable; section V (pp. 22-24) adds that all syllables have equal duration except long-vowel syllables, which 'also sound a little stronger', and that 1st person is marked by lengthening the last vowel of the verb/noun. No secondary stress or explicit exceptions.

sources.note: Comparative, not a description of nort2980 itself: pp. 124-125 note that in the Junín ('juninense') 1st-person forms with vowel length the accent falls on the final syllable ([wasí:], [pulí:]) unlike Ayacucho penult; sec. 4.5 (p. 128) says penultimate accent prevails in most Quechua varieties; ch. IX mentions Tarma oxytone forms arising from syllable reduction (cakrá-y < cakra-yki), citing Adelaar.
